Western Relocation Atlas

Eleven-state screen · home values as of August 2026

Western Relocation Atlas

Every census tract in the Mountain West, Washington, Oregon and California, scored on seven criteria and grouped into 148 areas. Of 15,188 populated tracts, 10,172 pass the budget and airport filters.

The WestWashingtonOregonCaliforniaMontanaIdahoWyomingColoradoUtahNevadaArizonaNew MexicoMethod

The West at a glance

  • Seven criteria, weighted your way. Live music; mountains; parks and shore; peace and quiet; schools; climate risk to mid-century; walkability. To start, mountains count double parks and the two together count the same as each of the others.
  • Scores are percentiles. Each criterion is ranked among all 15,188 tracts, 100 being best. A neighborhood’s score is the weighted average of the seven.
  • An area’s score is its three best neighborhoods. So a metro can lead on a handful of streets while most of it scores lower.
  • Two filters. A typical home value of $300k to $950k, and an airport with daily airline service within about 100 km.
  • Walkability means somewhere to walk to. Half is the EPA index; half is how close home is to a downtown, a main street or a corner of shops and cafes.

Your weights

    Set what matters to you. Move a slider and every table, state summary and map on this page is recalculated from all 15,188 neighborhoods.

    • The percentage is each criterion’s share of the score. A slider at zero leaves that criterion out.
    • Drag a row by its handle to change the column order in every table. “Weights from order” turns that order into 7-6-5-4-3-2-1 weights.
    • ▲ and ▼ beside a rank show how far the area has moved from its place at the original weights.
    • The Weights button in the bar above opens this panel from anywhere on the page. Your setting is kept in this browser where storage is allowed.

    Top twenty areas

    WA

    Washington

    • Pattern. Climate is the strength (88th percentile on average). Mountains are the weakness west of the Cascades, typically 23 km away.
    • East of the Cascades. The Tri-Cities, Yakima and Othello have almost no live music and heavy smoke.
    • Caveat. Wind comes from only six weather stations.

    Areas that pass both filters

    OR

    Oregon

    • Weak spot. Smoke. Eugene and Grants Pass have the worst readings in the screen, driven by the 2020 and 2022 fires. West of the Cascades the mountains are also 20–30 km away.
    • Caveats. Coast readings (Newport, Astoria) are borrowed from valley monitors 90 km away, so they are too high. There is no 2025 school data for Oregon.

    Areas that pass both filters

    CA

    California

    • In-budget weak spots. Schools: the typical in-budget neighborhood is 1.3 grades below the national average. Air: twice the ozone days of other states and a third more smoke and haze. Heat: most in-budget housing is inland.
    • Central Valley. Merced, Modesto, Bakersfield, Stockton and Fresno mostly face 80–125 very hot days by the 2050s.
    • Caveats. The climate score counts California’s rainless summer as dry-spell risk; that costs coastal areas such as Los Angeles a number of places. Central Valley heat estimates probably run 20–40 days high.

    Areas that pass both filters

    MT

    Montana

    • Pattern. Strong on schools, climate, quiet and mountains. Live music and walkability drop off sharply outside Missoula, Bozeman, Kalispell and Helena. Billings and Great Falls are far from mountains, with few venues.
    • Caveat. Bozeman’s air reading comes from monitors over 100 km away. Missoula and Bozeman both rely on regional airports.

    Areas that pass both filters

    ID

    Idaho

    • Pattern. Boise is near the top on music and mountains but only 35th percentile on climate (56 very hot days, smoke).
    • Snake River Plain. Twin Falls and Wendell are about 40 km from mountains, with below-average schools.

    Areas that pass both filters

    WY

    Wyoming

    • Pattern. Casper’s 12 mph average wind puts it in the 32nd percentile for quiet.
    • Caveat. Wind data covers only four Wyoming stations.

    Areas that pass both filters

    CO

    Colorado

    • Weak spots. Quiet (41st percentile: wind and big-metro density) and Front Range ozone: Boulder 15 days a year, Denver 11.
    • Caveat. Colorado’s 2025 school figures are estimated from state tests.

    Areas that pass both filters

    UT

    Utah

    • Pattern. The closest mountains of any state, typically 6 km. Quiet and air are the weak spots: 9 ozone days a year and winter haze in Salt Lake. St. George faces 113 very hot days by the 2050s.
    • Caveat. Wind for the whole Wasatch Front comes from one station.

    Areas that pass both filters

    NV

    Nevada

    • Pattern. Good on music and mountains. Weak on schools, quiet and heat: 130 very hot days for the typical neighborhood. Reno has heavy smoke.

    Areas that pass both filters

    AZ

    Arizona

    • Pattern. The weakest climate score of any state (24th percentile). Phoenix faces 163 very hot days and 15 ozone days a year. Flagstaff is strong on mountains and quiet, with schools half a grade below average.
    • Caveat. The mountain measure underrates Phoenix: its desert preserves are too small to register on a 4 km grid.

    Areas that pass both filters

    NM

    New Mexico

    • Pattern. Good music and mountains around Santa Fe and Albuquerque. Schools are the drag, typically 0.9 grades below average.
    • Caveat. Los Alamos has the best schools here (+1.7 grades), but the town-centre rule misses its downtown, so its walkability is understated.

    Method and limits

    • This is a first-pass screen. It uses region-wide stand-ins for the measures in the neighborhood study, so it is good for finding candidates and less good for ranking streets within a city.
    • Weights apply to the seven criteria. The mix inside a criterion (the four parts of climate, the two halves of walkability) and the two filters are fixed.
    • Mountains: distance from home to terrain standing 300–500 m higher, on a 4 km elevation grid. Narrow valleys and small desert ranges are underrated.
    • Parks and shore: the share of land within 1.5 km of home that is park or protected open space, plus a bonus for salt-water shore within 3 km. The inner bays of San Francisco Bay and south Puget Sound are not counted as shore.
    • Quiet: highway, rail and airport zones, the number of people living within 8 km, and average wind from airport weather stations. Station coverage is thin in Washington, Utah and Wyoming.
    • Music: a hand-built list of about 270 venues, with jazz rooms weighted higher and small-market rooms lower.
    • Climate: estimated days at or above 95°F by the 2050s, wildfire hazard, ozone and fine-particle readings for 2019–25, and dry spells. Heat estimates are rough in California’s interior valleys.
    • Town centres: a downtown needs shops and restaurants with civic offices alongside; a main street or corner needs a tight street grid or a neighborhood where at least a third of homes pre-date 1950.
    • Schools are grade levels above or below the national average for 2009–19. Colorado’s 2025 figures are estimated and Oregon has none.
    • Home value is Zillow’s neighborhood figure where one exists, otherwise the ZIP code’s. Airport distance is a straight line, so ferries and mountain passes are not accounted for except on the Olympic Peninsula.
